cues.text: ODYSSEY — BOOK XIX
The interview by the fire;\nthe scar; the contest announced.
But noble Odysseus stayed behind in the hall,\nplotting the suitors' slaughter with Athena's help.
At once he spoke winged words to Telemachus:
"Telemachus, the weapons of war must be laid away inside —
all of them; and the suitors — when they miss them\nand question you — talk them around with soft words:
'I laid them out of the smoke:\nthey no longer looked like the arms
Odysseus left behind when he went to Troy — they are\nfouled over, as far as the breath of the fire reached.
And a greater fear — this too\na god has cast into my heart:
that in your wine you might raise a quarrel among\nyou and wound one another, and shame the feast
and the wooing. For iron of itself draws a man on.'"\nSo he spoke; and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,
and calling out the nurse Eurycleia he said:
"Nurse, come — shut the women in their quarters for me\nuntil I have stowed away in the storeroom my father's
beautiful arms, which the smoke\ndulls, uncared for, all about
the house, since my father went away.\nI was still a child then.
Now I want to lay them where the\nbreath of the fire will not reach."
Then the dear nurse Eurycleia answered him:
"Yes, child — and if only you would\ntake up the good sense at last
to care for the house and guard all its possessions!
But come — who then will fetch\na light and carry it for you,
if the slave-women, who would\nhave lit you, may not come out?"
Then clear-headed Telemachus answered her:
"This stranger here. I will keep no man idle who\ntakes from my grain-measure, however far he has come."
So he spoke; and for her the word stayed wingless.
And she locked the doors of the well-settled halls.
Then the two sprang up, Odysseus and his shining son,\nand carried in the helmets and the bossed shields
and the sharp-pointed spears;\nand before them Pallas Athena,
holding a golden lamp, made a light most beautiful.
And suddenly Telemachus said to his father:
"Father — here is a great wonder my eyes look on!
The walls of the hall — no question — and the fine crossbeams,\nthe fir rafters, and the pillars rising high
shine in my eyes as if from a blazing fire.
Surely some god is in the house,\none of those who hold wide heaven."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered him:
"Quiet. Rein in your thought. Ask no questions.
This is the way of the gods who hold Olympus.
Go you to bed. I will remain behind here to stir\nthe slave-women a little more, and your mother:
in her grief she will ask me about every particular."
So he spoke; and Telemachus went out through the hall\nto his chamber, under the blazing torches, to lie down
where he always slept when sweet sleep came to him.
There he lay down now too, and waited for shining Dawn.
But noble Odysseus stayed behind in the hall,\nplotting the suitors' slaughter with Athena's help.
And out of her chamber came watchful-minded\nPenelope, like Artemis, or golden Aphrodite.
They set her chair, where she\nalways sat, beside the fire —
a chair wound round with ivory\nand silver, which the craftsman
Icmalius once made, and fixed beneath it a footrest
all of a piece with it,\nwhere a great fleece would be thrown.
There she sat down now, watchful-minded Penelope.
And the white-armed slave-women came in from the hall\nand cleared away the piles of bread, and the tables,
and the cups from which the overbearing men had drunk;
they raked the fire from the\nbraziers to the floor and stacked
fresh wood upon them, for light and for warmth.
And Melantho went at Odysseus a second time:
"Stranger — are you going to plague\nus even now, all through the night,
prowling around the house, spying on the women?
Out the door, you wretch —\nand be glad of the meal you got —
or you'll go out quick enough\nwith a torch-brand at your back!"
Then, glaring from under his brows,\nOdysseus of the many designs replied:
"Woman possessed — why go for me with a heart so angry?
Because I am dirty, because\nthe clothes on my body are bad,
because I beg through the land? Necessity is on me:
that is what beggars and wandering men are like.
I too once lived in a house among men, a fortunate\nman in a wealthy one, and I often gave to a wanderer,
whoever he might be and whatever need he came in.
Slaves I had past counting, and everything in plenty\nby which men live well and get the name of rich.
But Zeus the son of Cronos stripped it all —\nsuch, no doubt, was his will.
So look to yourself, woman: take care you never lose
all that shine of yours,\nthat sets you off among the slave-women —
in case your mistress turns on you in anger,\nor Odysseus comes. For a portion of hope is left.
And even if he is dead as you think, and past returning,\nby Apollo's grace there is his son by now,
such a son — Telemachus. Not one woman in these halls\nescapes his eye at her mischief. He is past that age."
So he spoke; and watchful-minded Penelope heard him,
and rounded on the handmaid,\nand spoke a word, and named her:
"Be sure of this, bold face,\ndog past all shame: your grand
performance is not lost on me —\nyou will wipe it off on your own head.
You knew — every part of it —\nyou heard it from my own mouth:
that I meant to question the stranger in my halls\nabout my husband, for whom I grieve past telling."
Then she spoke to Eurynome the housekeeper:
"Eurynome, bring up a bench, and a fleece on it,\nfor the stranger to sit and speak his word and hear me
out: I wish to question him through and through."
So she spoke; and the woman bustled to bring the polished\nbench and set it down, and threw a fleece upon it,
and there much-enduring noble Odysseus sat.
And watchful-minded Penelope began to speak among them:
"Stranger, this first will I myself ask you:
What man are you, and from where?\nWhere are your city and your parents?"
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Lady, no mortal man on the boundless earth could find\na fault in you: your fame goes up to the wide sky —
like the fame of some blameless king,\na god-fearing man ruling among many people and mighty,
upholding straight judgments; and the black earth bears
wheat and barley under him,\nand the trees hang heavy with fruit,
the flocks throw firm young, the sea yields fish,
all from his good governing;\nand under him the people flourish.
So — question me now on any\nother matter, here in your house,
but do not ask my race and my fathers' country,\nor you will fill my heart still fuller with pains
as I remember: I am a man of many\nsorrows. And there is no need
to sit in a stranger's house grieving and lamenting —\ngrief without respite makes everything worse —
and one of the slave-women might\ntake offense — or you yourself —
and say I swim in tears because\nthe wine has weighed my wits."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Stranger, my excellence — my face, my figure —\nthe deathless ones destroyed the day the Argives
boarded ship for Ilium, and my husband Odysseus with them.
If he came back — if he watched over this life of\nmine — my fame would be greater so, and lovelier.
Now I only grieve: so many evils the god has driven at me.
All the great men who hold power among the islands —\nDulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus —
and those whose homes are round clear-skied Ithaca itself:
they woo me against my will, and wear this house away.
So I pay no mind to strangers, none to suppliants,\nnone at all to heralds, the workers for the people;
no — longing for Odysseus melts the heart in me.
They press the marriage on;\nand I wind out my skein of tricks.
First it was the robe: a god breathed it into my heart —
to set up a great loom in the halls and weave at it,
fine-threaded, beyond all measure wide;\nand I told them straightway:
'Young men, my suitors — since noble Odysseus is dead,\nwait, though you burn for my wedding, till I finish
this cloth — let my spinning not be wasted on the wind —\na shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day
the ruinous doom of death that lays men low will take him:
let no Achaean woman in the land hold it against me
that a man who won so much should\nlie without his winding-sheet.'
So I spoke, and their proud hearts were persuaded.
Then every day I wove at the great loom,\nand every night I unwove it by torchlight.
Three years my trick escaped them,\nand I kept the Achaeans persuaded;
but when the fourth year came, as the seasons rolled on,
the months waning away,\nthe long tale of days accomplished,
then — through my slave-women, those careless bitches —\nthey came on me and caught me, and shouted me down.
So I finished it — against my will, under force.
And now I can neither escape the marriage nor\nfind any other design. My parents urge me hard
to marry; and my son chafes as these men eat his living —\nhe understands now: he is a man by now, fully able
to care for a house that Zeus grants glory to.
But even so, tell me your stock, where you are from:
you were not born of the oak in\nthe old tales, nor of a stone."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Honored wife of Laertes' son Odysseus,\nwill you not leave off asking me my lineage?
Well — I will tell you.\nThough truly you hand me over to sorrows
more than hold me now: that is the way of it,\nwhen a man has been gone from his country as long as I have,
wandering through many cities of men, suffering pains.
Even so, I will tell you what you ask and probe for.
There is a land called Crete, out in the wine-dark sea,
beautiful and rich, ringed by the water;\nand in it are people past counting, and ninety cities:
tongue mixed with tongue — Achaeans there,\ngreat-hearted native Cretans, Cydonians,
Dorians in their three clans, and noble Pelasgians;
and among the cities is Cnossus,\nthe great town, where Minos
was king by nine-year terms, great Zeus's intimate —\nthe father of my father, great-hearted Deucalion.
Deucalion fathered me, and lord Idomeneus;\nbut Idomeneus had gone in the beaked ships
to Ilium with the sons of Atreus.\nMy famous name is Aethon —
the younger brother by birth;\nhe was elder, and the better man.
There I saw Odysseus, and gave him guest-gifts:
for the strength of the wind had brought him down on Crete
as he made for Troy, driving him off course past Malea.
He anchored at Amnisus, by the cave of Eileithyia,
in that difficult harbor, and barely rode out the squalls.
He came straight up to the town, asking for Idomeneus:
his guest-friend, he said, beloved and honored.
But it was now the tenth dawn\nfor Idomeneus, or the eleventh,
since he had gone with the beaked ships to Ilium.
So I brought him to the house and gave him welcome,\nwarm and openhanded — the house had plenty in it —
and for the rest, for the\ncompanions who followed with him,
I gathered barley-meal from the\npublic store, and sparkling wine,
and oxen for sacrifice, till their hearts were satisfied.
Twelve days the noble Achaeans stayed with me,
pinned there: the great North Wind\nheld them, and would not let them
stand even on shore — some hard god had raised it.
On the thirteenth the wind dropped,\nand they put out to sea."
He made the many lies he told seem like the truth.
And as she listened her tears ran, and her flesh melted —
as snow melts away on the high crests of the mountains,\nsnow the West Wind piled and the East Wind thaws,
and as it melts the rivers run full with it:
so her beautiful cheeks melted with falling tears,
as she wept for her own husband —\nsitting at her side. And Odysseus
pitied his wife in his heart as she grieved,\nbut his eyes stood fixed as horn or iron,
unwavering in their lids: with craft he hid his tears.
And when she had taken her fill of tear-heavy mourning,\nshe found words again, and answered him:
"Now, stranger, I think I shall put you to the test:
whether you truly hosted my husband there in your\nhalls with his godlike companions, as you say.
Tell me what kind of clothes he wore on his body,
and what kind of man he was,\nand the companions who followed him."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Lady, that is hard — for one so long apart\nto say. It is the twentieth year already
since he went from there and left my country behind.
Even so I will tell you how my heart's eye pictures him.
Noble Odysseus wore a woolen mantle of sea-purple,
a double fold; and the brooch on it was fashioned of gold,
with paired sheaths for the pins;\nthe face of it was a marvel:
a hound held a dappled fawn between its forepaws,\ngripping it as it writhed. And everyone wondered at them —
both of gold: the one gripping the fawn and throttling it,
the fawn straining with its feet\nto escape, even as it struggled.
And I noticed the tunic on his body, all a-shimmer,\nlike the skin that slips from a dried onion:
that soft it was, and bright as the sun itself.
Many the women, I tell you, who gazed at him in wonder.
And another thing I will tell you:\nlay it up in your heart.
I do not know whether Odysseus\nwore these things from home,
or some companion gave them to him boarding the fast ship,
or perhaps some guest-friend, since to many men\nOdysseus was dear: few of the Achaeans were his equals.
I too gave him things: a sword of bronze,\na folded mantle, fine, sea-purple, and a fringed tunic,
and sent him off with honor on his well-benched ship.
Also a herald attended him, a little older than he was;\nand I will tell you what he looked like too:
round in the shoulders, dark-skinned, curly-headed,\nEurybates his name; and Odysseus prized him above
his other companions, for their minds ran matched.
So he spoke; and he stirred in her\nstill more the longing for weeping,
as she recognized the tokens Odysseus described so surely.
And when she had taken her fill of tear-heavy mourning,\nthen she found words again, and said to him:
"Now, stranger, pitiable as you were to me before,\nin my halls you shall be dear and honored.
It was I who gave him those clothes —\nI, the very clothes you speak of —
folded from the storeroom,\nand I pinned on the shining brooch
to be his jewel. And I shall never welcome him\nagain come home to his own dear fatherland.
By an evil fate Odysseus went in the hollow\nship to look on Evil-Ilium, never to be named."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Honored wife of Laertes' son Odysseus,\nmar your lovely skin no more, and melt your heart
no more away, weeping for your husband.\nNot that I blame you at all:
any woman mourns the husband she has lost,\nthe man of her youth, whose children she bore in love —
even a lesser man than Odysseus,\nwhom they call the equal of the gods.
But cease from weeping, and attend to my word:
for I will speak the exact truth and hide nothing:
I have already heard of Odysseus' homecoming —\nnear, in the rich land of the Thesprotian men,
alive; and he is bringing many fine treasures home,
begging his way through the country.\nBut his trusted companions
he lost, and the hollow ship, on the wine-dark sea,
on the way from the island of\nThrinacia: for Zeus and Helios
were set at odds with him —\nhis companions killed the Sun's cattle.
They all perished in the surging sea; but he rode\nthe keel of the ship, and the wave threw him ashore
on the land of the Phaeacians,\nwhose birth is next to the gods'.
They honored him from the heart like a god, and gave\nhim many things, and were themselves ready to bring him
home unharmed. And Odysseus would have been here
long since; but this seemed to\nhis heart the more profitable way:
to travel wide and gather wealth — for beyond all\nmortal men Odysseus knows the profitable turn:
no living man could rival him at that.
So Pheidon told me all of it,\nthe king of the Thesprotians;
and he swore an oath to me,\npouring the libation in his house,
that a ship was hauled down and a crew standing\nready to convey him home to his own dear fatherland.
But me he sent off first: for a Thesprotian ship\nhappened to be sailing for Dulichium, rich in wheat.
And he showed me all the treasure Odysseus had gathered:
truly it would feed a man's line to the tenth generation,
such a store of the lord's goods lay there in his halls.
Odysseus, he said, was gone to Dodona, to hear the\nwill of Zeus out of the god's own high-crowned oak:
how he should come home to his own dear fatherland,\nopenly or in secret, after so long away.
So he is safe; so he will come — and soon now,\nvery near: not far from his friends and his fathers' land
will he be for long. And still\nI will give you my oath on it.
Now Zeus be my witness first —\nhighest and best of the gods —
and the hearth of blameless Odysseus,\nto which I have come:
all this shall be accomplished exactly as I say.
Within this very turning of the\nlight Odysseus will be here:
between this month's waning and the rising of the next."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Ah, stranger, if only that word might be accomplished:
then you would quickly know my friendship, and gifts
in plenty from me — any man who\nmet you would call you blessed.
But this is how my heart forebodes it, and how it will be:
Odysseus is not coming home; and you will get no\npassage — for there are no masters in this house
such as Odysseus was among men — if he ever was —\nto welcome honored strangers, and to send them on.
But wash him, my handmaids, and lay out a bed:
bedstead and cloaks and shining blankets,\nso he may come warm through to Dawn of the golden throne.
And in the early morning bathe him and rub him with oil,
so that here inside, at Telemachus' side,\nhe may look to his dinner,
seated in the hall. And the worse for any man of them
who galls him — heart-destroyer: he will accomplish\nnothing here ever again, rage at it as he bitterly may.
Whether I stand out
at all among women in mind and thoughtful counsel,\nif all unwashed and badly dressed you sit at meat
in my halls? Men are creatures of a short day.
The man who is hard himself, and knows hard thoughts,\non him all mortals call down pains to come
while he lives, and when he is\ndead they mock him, every one;
but the man who is blameless himself,\nand knows blameless thoughts —
his fame the guests he served carry wide\nto all mankind, and many call him noble."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Honored wife of Laertes' son Odysseus,\ncloaks and shining blankets turned hateful to me
the day I first put the snowy mountains of Crete\nbehind me, going aboard the long-oared ship.
I will lie this night as I have lain\nthrough sleepless nights before:
many the nights I have spent on some rough bed,\nwaiting it out for shining fair-throned Dawn.
Nor do foot-washings bring my heart any pleasure:
no woman shall touch this foot of mine\nof all those who serve about your house —
unless there is some old woman, old and faithful-hearted,
who has endured in her spirit as much as I have endured:
such a one I would not grudge the touching of my feet."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Dear stranger — no man so discerning, of all the guests\nfrom far lands, ever came more welcome to my house:
so shaped and thought-through is everything you say.
I have an old woman whose breast is packed with counsel,
who nursed and reared that unlucky man, my husband —\ntook him into her arms the hour his mother bore him:
she will wash your feet, feeble with age though she is.
Up now, watchful-minded Eurycleia:
wash him — a man the same age as\nyour master. And perhaps Odysseus
by now is like him in his feet, like him in his hands:
for in misfortune mortal men age fast."
So she spoke; and the old woman hid her face in her hands
and shed hot tears, and gave voice to words of mourning:
"Ah me, child, and I helpless for you! Truly Zeus
hated you beyond all men —\nand yours was a god-fearing heart.
For no mortal ever burned to Zeus who delights in\nthunder so many fat thigh-pieces, such choice hecatombs,
as you gave him, praying you might come to\na sleek old age and raise your shining son.
And now from you alone he has\ncut off the day of homecoming.
So too, I suppose, the women mocked him —
women of strangers in far lands,\nwhen he came to some man's famous house —
just as these bitches here mock you, all of them together:
it is to dodge their insults, their crowd of taunts,
that you will not let the women wash you.\nAnd I — not at all unwilling —
am ordered to it by Icarius' daughter,\nwatchful-minded Penelope.
So I will wash your feet — for Penelope's own sake and\nfor yours as well; for the heart within me is stirred
with sorrows. But come — take in the word I say:
many a travel-worn stranger has come to this house,\nbut never, I tell you, have I seen such a likeness
as you have — in body, in voice, in feet — to Odysseus."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Old mother, so they all say who have seen the two of us
with their own eyes: that we are very like each\nother — just as you yourself observe, and say."
So he spoke; and the old woman took the shining\nbasin she used for washing feet, and poured in water,
cold in plenty, then added hot to it. And Odysseus
sat down at the hearth —\nand swung round quickly toward the dark,
for a fear came over his heart that as she took hold\nshe might mark the scar, and the whole work come open.
She came close and began to wash\nher master. And at once she knew
the scar — the wound the boar\ndealt him with its white tusk
when he went to Parnassus, to Autolycus and his sons,\nhis mother's noble father, who outdid all men
in thievery and the oath: the god himself had\ngiven it him; to him he burned welcome thigh-pieces
of lambs and of kids, and the\ngod companioned him with a will.
Once Autolycus, coming to the rich land of Ithaca,\nfound his daughter's son a baby newly born;
and Eurycleia laid the child on his knees as he\nfinished supper, and spoke a word, and named him:
"Autolycus — find the name yourself, to give your\nown child's child. He is a child of many prayers."
Then Autolycus answered her and said:
"Son-in-law and daughter, give him the name I say.
Since I have come to this place at odds with many —\nwith men and with women across the nourishing earth —
let Odysseus, Man at Odds, be the name he carries.
And for my part: when he is grown, and comes to Parnassus,
to his mother's great house, where my possessions are,\nI will give him a share and send him home rejoicing."
For those gifts Odysseus went:\nto receive his shining presents.
And Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus clasped his\nhands in welcome, and greeted him with honeyed words;
and Amphithea, his mother's mother,\nfolding Odysseus in her arms,
kissed his head, and both his beautiful eyes.
Then Autolycus called to his glorious sons to\nmake the meal ready; and they heard his urging:
at once they led in a bull of five years,\nflayed it and dressed it, and split the whole in pieces,
and jointed the meat with skill,\nand fixed it on the spits,
and roasted it with care, and shared out all the portions.
So then, the whole day long until the setting of the sun,
they feasted; and no man's appetite\nwent short of the equal feast.
And when the sun went down and the dusk came on,\nthey lay down then, and took the gift of sleep.
When Dawn appeared, the early-born, with fingers of rose,
they went their way to the hunt — the hounds and with them
the sons of Autolycus themselves; and noble Odysseus
went along with them.\nThey climbed the steep mountain, mantled
in forest — Parnassus —\nand soon they reached its windy folds.
The sun was just striking the plowlands,\nrising out of the deep smooth stream of Ocean,
when the beaters came to a glen; ahead of them ran\nthe hounds, casting for the scent, and behind them
came the sons of Autolycus; and noble Odysseus
moved close behind the hounds,\nswinging his long-shadowed spear.
There, in a dense thicket, lay couched a great boar.
No force of wet-blowing winds could pierce that covert,\nno shaft of the shining sun could strike into it,
no rain drive through it, so dense it was,\nand the fallen leaves lay heaped in it past counting.
Around the boar came the din of feet — men's and hounds' —
as they pressed in on him; and out of his lair, head-on,
bristles ridged on his neck, fire standing in his eyes,\nhe stood at bay, close in. And first of all Odysseus
rushed him, the long spear high in his heavy hand,\nhungry to strike; but the boar was quicker — gashed him
above the knee, charging in slantwise, and ripped away
a long gouge of flesh with his tusk:\nbut it did not reach the bone.
And Odysseus struck home on the right shoulder,\nand the point of the shining spear went through and through:
down in the dust he went, bleating,\nand the life flew out of him.
Then the dear sons of Autolycus\nbusied themselves with the carcass,
and the wound of blameless, godlike Odysseus they bound\nwith skill, and with a chanted spell they stanched
And Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus\nhealed him well, and gave him shining gifts,
and quickly sent him back\nrejoicing to his own dear country,
to Ithaca. And his father and his honored mother
rejoiced at his homecoming,\nand questioned him on everything —
the scar, and what had happened;\nand he told them all of it well:
how the boar's white tusk had gashed him at the hunt\non his climb up Parnassus with the sons of Autolycus.
That scar — as the old woman took\nhis leg in the flat of her hands
she knew it under her fingers. She let the foot drop:
the shin fell in the basin; the bronze rang out;
the basin tipped over sideways,\nand the water ran on the ground.
And joy and anguish seized her mind at once:\nher eyes filled up with tears; her welling voice stuck fast.
She touched Odysseus on the chin, and said:
"You are Odysseus — dear child! And I did not know you,\nnot before I had handled all of him — my master."
She spoke, and her eyes went toward Penelope,\nready to tell her that her own husband was in the house.
But Penelope could not meet the look or take its meaning,\nfor Athena had turned her mind away. And Odysseus,
feeling for her throat, caught it with his right hand,
and with the other pulled her closer to him, and said:
"Nurse — why would you destroy me? You yourself nursed me
at this breast of yours. Now, after suffering many pains,
I have come in the twentieth year to my fathers' land.
But since you have found it out,\nand a god has put it in your heart,
be silent — let no one else in the halls learn of it.
For I will say this outright, and it will be accomplished:
if a god brings the haughty suitors down beneath my hands,
I will not spare even you, my nurse though you are,\nthat day I kill the other slave-women in my halls."
Then watchful-minded Eurycleia answered him:
"My child, what a word has\nslipped the fence of your teeth!
You know my strength — how it stands and will not bend:
I will hold like solid stone, like iron.
And another thing I will tell you:\nlay it up in your heart.
If a god brings the haughty\nsuitors down beneath your hands,
then I will name you the women of the halls, every one:
which of them dishonor you, and which are guiltless."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Nurse, why would you name them? There is no need.
I will observe them well myself, and learn each one.
No — keep the story silent. Leave it to the gods."
So he spoke; and the old woman went off through the hall
to fetch fresh water for his feet:\nthe first was all spilled.
And when she had washed him and rubbed him richly with oil,\nOdysseus drew his bench again nearer the fire
to warm himself, and covered the scar with his rags.
And watchful-minded Penelope began to speak among them:
"Stranger, one small thing more I will ask you myself —\nfor soon enough now comes the hour of sweet rest,
for whomever sweet sleep will take, however careworn.
But to me the god has dealt grief past measuring:
by day my one delight is weeping and lamenting,
while I look to my work and the\nwork of my women in the house;
but when night comes, and rest takes all the others,\nI lie in my bed, and crowding round my beating heart
the sharp anxieties torment me as I mourn.
As when the daughter of Pandareus,\nthe pale-green nightingale,
sings beautifully at the first new standing of spring,\nperched in the thick leafage of the trees,
and pouring, turning, threads her many-noted voice,
mourning her child, her beloved Itylus,\nwhom once with the bronze
she killed in her blindness of\nmind — the son of lord Zethus:
so my heart too is torn two ways, this way and that:
do I stay by my son and keep everything unmoved —\nmy goods, my slave-women, the great high-roofed house —
respecting my husband's bed and the voice of the people;
or do I follow now whichever of the Achaeans is best
among my suitors in the halls,\nand offers bride-gifts past counting?
My son — while he was still a child, and soft in mind,
he would not have me marry and leave my husband's house;
but now that he is grown, come to the measure of manhood,\nhe prays me to go back home, out of these halls —
chafing over the estate the Achaeans eat away.
But come — hear this dream of mine, and read it for me.
I keep twenty geese about the house; they eat wheat\nsoftened in water, and it warms me to watch them.
And out of the mountain came a great hook-beaked eagle
and broke all their necks,\nand killed them; and they lay strewn
in a heap through the halls,\nwhile he was borne up to the bright sky.
And I wept — I wailed aloud, though it was a dream,\nand around me gathered the fair-braided Achaean women,
as I grieved most pitiably because\nthe eagle had killed my geese.
But back he came, and perched on the jut of the roof-beam,\nand with a man's voice he checked my grieving:
'Take heart, daughter of far-famed Icarius:
this is no dream but a waking sight —\na good one, and it shall be accomplished.
The geese are the suitors; and I — I was the eagle-bird
before; but now I have come back, and I am your husband,
and I will let loose an ugly doom on all the suitors.'
So he spoke; and the honey-sweet sleep let me go;\nand casting about, I saw the geese there in the halls
pecking their wheat beside the trough,\njust where they always were."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Lady, there is no way to wrench this dream aside\nto read it another way: Odysseus himself, no other,
has shown you how he will end it:\ndestruction shows plain for the suitors —
for every man of them; not one shall\nslip out of death and the fates."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Stranger, dreams are hopeless things,\nand their talk past sorting;
not everything in them is accomplished for mortals.
For two are the gates of strengthless dreams:
one pair is fashioned of horn, and one of ivory.
Those dreams that come through the gate of sawn ivory
cheat and beguile: they carry words that come to nothing.
But those that come out through the gate of polished horn
accomplish true things, whenever a mortal sees them.
But my strange dream, I fear, did not come from there —\nah, welcome as that would be to me and to my child.
And another thing I will tell you:\nlay it up in your heart.
Here now comes the dawn of the evil name, that will cut me
away from the house of Odysseus.\nFor now I will set the contest:
the axes he used to stand up in a row in his halls,\nlike the props of a ship on the stocks — twelve in all;
and standing far back he would\nshoot an arrow through them.
Now I will set this contest before the suitors:
whoever strings the bow most easily in his hands,\nand shoots an arrow through all twelve axes —
him I will follow, forsaking this house, this house\nof my marriage, this beautiful house, full of all
that sustains life. I think I shall\nremember it even in my dreams."
Then Odysseus of the many designs answered her:
"Honored wife of Laertes' son Odysseus,\ndo not put off this contest in your house one hour.
For Odysseus of the many designs will be here first —
before these men, handling and handling the polished bow,\ncan string the cord and shoot through the iron."
Then watchful-minded Penelope answered him:
"Stranger, if you were only\nwilling to sit by me in the halls
and give me pleasure, sleep would never settle on my eyes.
But there is no way men can go sleepless forever:
the deathless ones have set a portion for each\nthing mortals do on the grain-giving earth.
So I will go up now to my upper room to lie on\nthe bed that has become a bed of groaning for me,
forever stained with my tears, since the day Odysseus\nwent to look on Evil-Ilium, never to be named.
There I will lie; and you lie down in this house —
spread something on the floor, or let them set you a bed."
So speaking she climbed to her shining upper room,\nnot alone: her handmaids went up with her.
Climbing to her upper room with her serving-women,\nshe wept there for Odysseus, her dear husband, until
gray-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep upon her eyelids.
